nameStory: The European Starling gets its name from its Old English roots — 'starling' comes from 'staer,' meaning 'starling,' with the diminutive '-ling' ending. They're called 'European' in North America to distinguish them from native species, since these birds were introduced from Europe in the 1890s. A group of Shakespeare enthusiasts released 60 of them in New York's Central Park, hoping to introduce every bird mentioned in the playwright's works!
description: European Starlings are chunky, medium-sized birds about the size of a robin — roughly 8 inches long with a stocky build. They have glossy black feathers that shimmer with green and purple metallic sheens in good light, often speckled with white spots that are most prominent in fall and winter. Their bills change color dramatically with the seasons, turning bright yellow in breeding season and dark in winter. These highly social birds are famous for their incredible mimicry abilities and massive flocks that create swirling, shape-shifting murmurations in the sky.

idTips.label: Glossy black plumage with metallic sheen
idTips.description: The feathers have an oily, iridescent quality that flashes green and purple in sunlight — like an oil slick on water

idTips.label: Seasonal bill color change
idTips.description: Bright corn-yellow bills in spring and summer turn dark blackish-brown in fall and winter

idTips.label: White speckled appearance
idTips.description: Fresh fall and winter feathers have crisp white tips that make the bird look heavily spotted, like someone flicked white paint on them

idTips.label: Pink-orange legs
idTips.description: Legs are noticeably pink to orange-pink year-round, contrasting with the dark body

idTips.label: Chunky, compact build
idTips.description: Stockier than most songbirds with a thick neck and relatively short tail that gives them a 'bowling pin' silhouette

idTips.label: Pointed, straight bill
idTips.description: Long, sharp, dagger-like bill that's perfectly straight — ideal for probing into grass and soil

habitat: European Starlings thrive in human-modified landscapes throughout New England — look for them in suburban lawns, city parks, agricultural fields, and shopping center parking lots. They prefer open areas with short grass for foraging, combined with nearby cavities for nesting in buildings, nest boxes, or tree holes. You'll rarely find them in deep forests, but they're abundant anywhere people live, from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Bills turn brilliant yellow and the white speckles largely disappear, revealing the full glossy black breeding plumage. Listen for their complex songs that include mimicked sounds of other birds, car alarms, and cell phone rings.
seasonality.summer: At peak glossiness with yellow bills and metallic sheen most prominent. Young birds appear brown and streaky, quite different from adults, and family groups forage together on lawns.
seasonality.fall: Fresh feathers create heavy white speckling that makes them look almost polka-dotted. Large flocks begin forming and bills start darkening from yellow to black.
seasonality.winter: Most heavily speckled appearance with dark bills. Massive flocks create spectacular murmurations at roost sites, often numbering in the thousands and performing aerial ballets at dusk.

funFact: European Starlings can perfectly mimic over 20 different bird species plus mechanical sounds like car alarms, chainsaws, and cell phones — some have even been taught to speak human words and have been recorded 'talking' to each other in human speech!
confusionNotes: Young starlings in summer look completely different — brown and streaky like large sparrows. Adult starlings are often confused with grackles, but grackles are much larger with longer tails and lack the white speckling. Remember: if it's robin-sized with a straight bill and looks 'sparkly,' it's probably a starling.
contextualKnowledge: European Starlings are considered an invasive species in North America, introduced in 1890-1891 by the American Acclimatization Society. Despite being non-native, they're now one of the most abundant birds in North America with an estimated population of 200 million. Their success comes at the cost of native cavity-nesting birds like bluebirds and woodpeckers, which they often outcompete for nesting sites.
compareHints: European Starlings are the only members of their genus in New England, making them unique among starlings here. Compared to similar-sized dark birds like grackles or blackbirds, starlings are much more compact and stocky with shorter tails. Unlike the uniform dark plumage of grackles, starlings have that distinctive white speckling in fall and winter, and their bills are straighter and more pointed than the slightly curved bills of most blackbirds.
